It's a small, five-file Node service. Here's how the pieces connect. ```mermaid flowchart LR server["server.js
HTTP + auth gate"] --> routes["routes.js
route table"] routes --> cache["cache.js
LRU read cache"] routes --> store["store.js
in-memory store"] cache --> store server --> auth["auth.js
token check"] ``` `server.js` opens the HTTP port and checks every request's bearer token through `auth.js` before anything else runs. `auth.js` signs and verifies tokens as `userId.signature`, using an HMAC secret from `AUTH_SECRET`. Once a request is authenticated, `routes.js` matches it against a small table of three endpoints: `GET /users`, `GET /orders`, `POST /orders`. Reads go through `cache.js`, a 256-entry LRU with no expiry of its own. Everything ultimately lands in `store.js`, an in-memory map where each record expires 15 minutes after it's last written. One thing to know: `routes.js` claims writes "invalidate the affected keys," but `POST /orders` never actually clears the cache. A stale order list can stick around until it ages out of the LRU on its own.
